paper_title: MMEnterprise-Bench: Evaluating Enterprise Agents over Evolving Multimodal Records

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Enterprise agents answer questions over workplace records that evolve through team collaboration. As information is shared, corrected, and revised across documents, chats, and figures, multiple versions of the same information accumulate in the workspace. Reliable question answering therefore requires agents to reason over sufficient evidence, resolve cross-source and temporal conflicts, and recognize when the available evidence is insufficient to establish an answer. To systematically evaluate these capabilities, we introduce MMEnterprise-Bench, a benchmark comprising 1,613 questions grounded in evolving multimodal records from simulated collaboration projects, covering three categories: Evidence Reasoning, Conflict Resolution, and Unanswerability. We evaluate 10 proprietary and open-source multimodal LLMs and find that even the strongest models struggle when evidence contains cross-source or temporal conflicts or spans multiple images. Moreover, increasing the retrieval budget or employing a larger retriever improves evidence recall but does not consistently translate into higher answer accuracy. These findings highlight the persistent challenges of reasoning over evolving workplace records and establish MMEnterprise-Bench as a testbed for developing more reliable enterprise agents. Code and data are available at https://mlvlab.github.io/MMEnterprise-Bench/.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large language model (LLM)-based enterprise agents are increasingly adopted to answer questions over enterprise workspaces, where knowledge is distributed across diverse sources, e.g., chats, emails, figures, reports, and slides. As teams collaborate, results are shared, questioned, and corrected, with updates propagating to subsequent sources *Equal contribution. Corresponding author. Figure 1: Conflicts across evolving multimodal records in MMEnterprise-Bench. Enterprise agents struggle with cross-source conflicts (top), in which different sources contain inconsistent versions of the same information, and temporal conflicts (bottom), in which records undergo multiple revisions over time. while earlier records remain unchanged. This process gives rise to two distinct types of conflicts, as illustrated in Fig. 1. First, cross-source conflict arises when different sources contain inconsistent versions of the same information. For example, an accuracy value may be corrected in Slack and email and subsequently updated in revised data sheet, while earlier records in Notion continue to reflect the original value. Second, temporal conflict arises when answering query requires recovering information from specific historical state rather than simply using its latest version. For instance, user may ask for the version immediately preceding particular modification in report that has undergone multiple revisions. Consequently, enterprise agents must provide reliable answers grounded not only in the correct information across multimodal sources, but also in its appropriate temporal state. Eight task types fall into three categories: Evidence Reasoning (ER) for deriving answers from sufficient evidence, Conflict Resolution (CR) for resolving conflicting evidence, and Unanswerability (UNS) for identifying questions that cannot be answered due to insufficient evidence. Building on these challenges, we evaluate three key capabilities of enterprise agents, i.e., (1) Evidence Reasoning (ER): answering from sufficient evidence over enterprise records, (2) Conflict Resolution (CR): resolving cross-source and temporal conflicts in the evidence, and (3) Unanswerability (UNS): recognizing when the available evidence is insufficient to establish an answer. These capabilities are particularly challenging in multimodal enterprise workspaces, where relevant evidence may appear in figures while subsequent corrections are communicated through textual records. Although recent enterprise QA benchmarks simulate workplace corpora (Choubey et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026), existing work does not explicitly address conflicts that arise across diverse multimodal sources and their evolving records. To this end, we introduce MMEnterpriseBench, comprising 1,613 QA pairs over evolving multimodal workplace records that are revised across sources, including questions that explicitly target their revision histories. MMEnterpriseBench evaluates enterprise agents across three dimensions, encompassing eight subtask types, as summarized in Tab. 1. We construct the benchmark by simulating collaborative enterprise workspaces across 30 projects grounded in textual and visual materials from public papers and reports. Within each project, collaborative events, such as result sharing, error detection, and correction, are instantiated through messages, emails, meeting notes, trackers, reports, and slides containing figures and tables. Crucially, earlier records across modalities are retained rather than overwritten, allowing superseded values to remain accessible within retrieval corpus of 7,140 textual and visual records shared across projects. This design preserves both inconsistent evidence across sources and multiple temporal states of the same information, thereby instantiating cross-source and temporal conflicts. We evaluate 10 proprietary and open-source multimodal LLMs as enterprise agents in retrievalaugmented generation (RAG) setting over simulated enterprise records. The strongest model, GPT5.6 Sol, achieves only 52.6% and 68.0% accuracy with 10 and 50 retrieved records, respectively. Performance on the CR category remains particularly low, ranging from 11.8% to 36.3% on cross-source conflicts and from 13.2% to 33.5% on temporal conflicts. Performance further degrades when answering questions requires reasoning across multiple visual sources. GPT-5.6 Sol achieves only 27.5% on questions requiring multiple images, compared with 83.3% on those grounded in single textual record. These findings highlight the limitations of current enterprise agents in resolving conflicting evidence across sources and over time, as well as reasoning across multiple visual records. (2) MMEnterprise-Bench evaluates three key capabilities of enterprise agents: Evidence Reasoning, Conflict Resolution, and Unanswerability, capturing cross-source and temporal conflicts across evolving multimodal sources. (3) We evaluate 10 enterprise agents and find that even the strongest models fall well short of reliable performance, particularly when evidence contains cross-source or temporal conflicts or spans multiple visual records.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Multimodal models for document understanding. Document understanding has been extensively studied through visual question answering over scanned documents, infographics, charts, and slides (Mathew et al., 2021, 2022; Masry et al., 2022; Tanaka et al., 2023). Subsequent benchmarks extend this setting to multi-page and longdocument scenarios, requiring models to locate and integrate evidence across pages, tables, and figures (Tito et al., 2023; Van Landeghem et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2025). In these benchmark settings, general-purpose multimodal LLMs have demonstrated strong performance by directly processing text-rich images and long interleaved multimodal inputs (Liu et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b). More recently, agentic approaches have further decomposed document question answering into multi-stage pipelines involving retrieval, visual inspection, and crossmodal evidence aggregation, performed by one or more models (Han et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a). Enterprise question answering benchmarks. Enterprise QA requires grounding answers in private, heterogeneous workplace records that are often redundant and uncurated. Recent benchmarks simulate such environments using synthetic documents, chats, emails, meetings, and tickets (Choubey et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026; Varhade et al., 2026; Vishwakarma et al., 2025; Abaskohi et al., 2026), but they are largely text-only and rarely treat earlier states of revised records as valid answers. For example, EnterpriseRAG-Bench (Sun et al., 2026) introduces fact-altered near-duplicates but accepts only the up-to-date value as correct, while WinSyn (Varhade et al., 2026) incorporates correctionchain distractors without altering the gold answers. Workplace agent benchmarks (Drouin et al., 2024; Styles et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025) instead emphasize tool-based task completion rather than evidence-grounded QA. Temporal knowledge benchmarks (Chen et al., 2021; Zhang and Choi, 2021; Vu et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025; Sobhani et al., 2026; Huwiler et al., 2025) evaluate factual validity over time, but primarily target public knowledge, personal conversations, or formally versioned documents, and are limited In contrast, as summarized in Tab. 2, to text. MMEnterprise-Bench evaluates both cross-source and temporal conflicts over multimodal workplace records grounded in real documents, where collaborative revisions spread across sources and modalities while preserving earlier states that may themselves constitute valid answers.

sections.title: 3 MMEnterprise-Bench
sections.content: MMEnterprise-Bench evaluates QA over shared workspace of evolving multimodal records. We first describe the construction of the simulated enterprise workspace and its annotations, as in Fig. 2. We then present our procedure for improving annotation quality and report the annotation statistics.

sections.title: 3.1 Enterprise Workspace Simulation
sections.content: In MMEnterprise-Bench, record denotes an individual item produced during simulated collaboration, such as message, an email, or figure. project is the basis of simulated collaboration, grounded in one of 30 seed documents drawn from public papers and reports, and comprises diverse collaborative events. The workspace aggregates records from all projects, representing the entire simulated enterprise and serving as the shared retrieval corpus for evaluation. Multimodal record generation. We extract text, tables, and figures from each seed document and Figure 2: MMEnterprise-Bench construction pipeline. Each seed document serves as the information source for project. Based on the extracted information and the projects context, we generate collaborative events and their corresponding records over time. These projects collectively form shared workspace of evolving multimodal records that contain cross-source and temporal conflicts. We then generate and validate questions grounded in this workspace to evaluate evidence reasoning, conflict resolution, and unanswerability. structure its key values, configurations, claims, and visual information. The extracted methods and results serve as the technical content for constructing heterogeneous workplace records, including messages, emails, meeting notes, and attached files. For visual artifacts, we reuse figures from the seed documents, render tables and charts from structured values, and compose reports and slides. Collaborative event generation within project. An event is workplace action performed by specified collaborator at specified time, such as reporting result, identifying an error, issuing correction, or making decision. Events serve as planning units, while records are their realizations, e.g., result-sharing event may be realized as message with an attached table. Based on this distinction, an LLM plans how information is introduced, shared, and revised throughout the project, including result releases, corrections, changes in work status, and document revisions, and represents these developments as collaborative events. We then organize the events chronologically. For example, typical sequence may involve collaborators sharing an incorrect value, detecting and confirming the error, and subsequently reporting the corrected value. Overall, these events define the temporal ordering and content relationships among records within each project. Workspace construction. The workspace serves as the environment in which all projects take place. For each project, we create team and specify roles, communication channels, access relationships, and deadlines, which collectively constrain who performs each event, when it occurs, and where the resulting records appear. This workspace-level structure grounds collaborative events in realistic organizational and access constraints. Earlier records and document versions are retained after revisions rather than overwritten, preserving both historical states and the progression of changes over time.

sections.title: 3.3 Quality Control and Human Validation
sections.content: We validate QA annotations through multi-stage pipeline comprising independent LLM-based assessments, complemented by blind human validation. For records, validation checks consistency with the source information and planned events, including temporal and access constraints. For QA annotations, validation verifies whether the cited evidence is sufficient to derive the reference answer and checks for ambiguous questions, incorrect reference answers, and answer leakage. Annotations that fail validation are revised or discarded. The validation prompts are provided in Appendix C.2. To assess the reliability of our LLM-based validation, we conduct human validation on subset of 100 QA annotations, comprising 50 LLM-accepted and 50 LLM-rejected annotations. Three annotators review each item without access to the LLMs decision. We classify an item as human-rejected if at least one annotator rejects it. As shown in Tab. 4, none of the 50 LLM-accepted items was rejected by any annotator, and all 29 human-rejected items were also rejected by the LLM. These results suggest that our LLM-based validation aligns with human judgments while applying more conservative acceptance criterion.

sections.title: 3.4 Dataset Statistics
sections.content: The benchmark contains 1,613 questions across 30 projects and 7,140 retrieval records, comprising 5,725 textual records and 1,415 visual records. The visual records include 658 PDF pages, 372 slides, and 385 standalone images or attachments. The corpus further contains 287 record versions, including 204 PDFs and 60 presentations. Each project contains 203 274 records, with median of 237. The question set comprises 1,526 answerable and 87 unanswerable questions across the three evaluation dimensions. For answerable questions, the gold evidence contains an average of 1.94 retrieval units per question, with 749 questions requiring one unit, 495 requiring two units, and 282 requiring three or more units. Moreover, 461 answerable questions (30.2%) span multiple source types. Detailed statistics are provided in Tab. 3.

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: We evaluate 10 open-source and proprietary models using {10, 50} retrieved records. For each question, Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B (Li et al., 2026) retrieves the top-k records from the workspace, which are then presented to the model ordered by timestamp and ID. To ensure consistent evaluation, we use GPT-5.6 Luna as an automatic judge, given the question, reference answer, and model response. We report overall and task-level accuracy across all 1,613 questions.

sections.title: 4.3 Analysis of Gold Evidence Records
sections.content: We analyze performance by the number and modality of gold evidence records required for each question under = 10 retrieval. Results by number of required gold evidence records. Tab. 6 shows that, for both text-only and image-only questions, all evaluated models perform worse when multiple evidence records are required than when single record suffices. For GPT-5.6 Sol, accuracy decreases from 83.3% to 51.5% for text-only questions and from 52.9% to 27.5% for image-only questions when moving from single-record to multi-record evidence. These gaps indicate that even powerful enterprise agents struggle to identify, aggregate, and jointly reason over evidence distributed across multiple records. Results by gold evidence modality. Beyond the number of required records, Tab. 6 shows that their modality introduces an additional source of difficulty. For GPT-5.6 Sol, accuracy on singlerecord questions is 83.3% with textual evidence but only 52.9% with visual evidence. The gap persists for multi-record questions, where accuracy is 51.5% for text-only evidence, 27.5% for image-only evidence, and 25.6% for mixed text and image evidence. Other models exhibit similar degradation on multi-record questions involving visual or mixed-modality evidence. These results show that, beyond aggregating information across records, reasoning over multimodal evidence remains substantial challenge for enterprise agents on MMEnterprise-Bench. sections.title: 4.4 Analysis on Record Retrieval
sections.content: In Tab. 7, we scale the number of retrieved records up to 100 and the retriever size up to 8B. We first examine whether retrieving more records improves QA accuracy as evidence recall increases. Although increasing consistently raises evidence recall, it does not always improve QA accuracy. With the 2B retriever, increasing from 50 to 100 raises recall from 57.0% to 64.8%, while Qwen3.52B accuracy decreases from 25.0% to 22.2%. Similarly, with the 8B retriever, recall increases from 59.6% to 67.3%, whereas InternVL3.5-8B accuracy decreases from 38.0% to 37.6%. We next verify the effect of retriever size by comparing the 2B and 8B retrievers. Compared with the 2B retriever, the 8B retriever consistently achieves higher recall, with gains of 1.7%, 2.6%, and 2.5% at = 10, 50, and 100, respectively. However, these recall gains do not consistently translate into higher QA accuracy. At = 100, GPT-5.6 Sol improves from 75.9% to 77.2% with the larger retriever, whereas Qwen3.5-4B declines from 46.9% to 46.6%. Overall, these results indicate that, for smaller models, higher evidence recall alone is insufficient to ensure improved QA performance.

sections.title: 4.5 Qualitative Analysis
sections.content: Fig. 3 illustrates two representative cases involving cross-source and temporal conflicts. Cross-source conflict. In Fig. 3 (left), corrections are communicated through Slack and revised documents, while the corresponding Notion records are updated at different times, leaving multiple conflicting values in the workspace. An interview count is corrected from 43 to 34 in revised memo, which also introduces new evidence row with value of 23. Meanwhile, the corresponding Notion entry retains an earlier value of 32 until later update. The question specifically asks for the value in the newly added row, requiring the model to track revisions across sources and distinguish the target value from other related updates rather than simply retrieve matching number. Even GPT-5.6 Sol, the strongest-performing model in our evaluation, incorrectly answers 34 instead of 23. Temporal conflict. Fig. 3 (right) presents deadline revised from September 1 at 20:00 to September 2 at 18:00, with both values preserved in the conversation history. The two questions ask for the current deadline and the deadline immediately preceding the revision, respectively. While the model correctly answers the first question, it returns the revised deadline for the second, despite the earlier value being available in the records. These failures highlight the difficulty of identifying the appropriate evidence among conflicting records and recovering the temporal state specified by the question when multiple historical versions remain accessible.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduce MMEnterprise-Bench, benchmark for evaluating question answering over evolvIt contains ing multimodal workplace records. 1,613 questions across 30 simulated collaboration projects grounded in public papers and reports, spanning three evaluation dimensions: Evidence Reasoning (ER), Conflict Resolution (CR), and Unanswerability (UNS). Our comprehensive evaluation of 10 proprietary and open-source enterprise agents reveals persistent challenges in integrating evidence across records and modalities, resolving cross-source and temporal conflicts, and recognizing insufficient information. Moreover, improved retrieval does not consistently translate into better QA performance, highlighting the need for models that can reason over multimodal evidence and evolving record states. MMEnterprise-Bench provides testbed for developing reliable enterprise assistants capable of answering questions as workplace information evolves.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: MMEnterprise-Bench uses simulated workplace records grounded in 30 public papers and reports. While designed to reflect realistic workplace collaboration, these records may not capture every aspect of real enterprise environments. Human validation showed high agreement for LLM-accepted annotations, although LLM-based generation and validation may still leave residual errors.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: MMEnterprise-Bench aims to support reliable enterprise assistants through evaluation on simulated workplace records. Benchmark performance does not guarantee reliability in real deployments, where privacy, access controls, and human oversight remain important. Artifacts. The benchmark is grounded in public papers and reports, with source and license information provided in Appendix A. Reuse and distribution must respect applicable licenses and attribution requirements. Workplace communications are simulated, and human validation was performed by the authors without recruiting external annotators. AI assistance. LLMs were used for data generation, validation, and answer evaluation, as described in Section 3 and Appendices B, C, and D. AI assistance was also used to draft and revise manuscript text and to assist with code development. The authors retain responsibility for all content, code, results, and claims.

sections.title: B Benchmark Construction Prompts
sections.content: This section presents the prompt templates used for enterprise workspace simulation and QA annotation in MMEnterprise-Bench. Each project is grounded in seed document, and the workspace aggregates records from all projects. Construction begins with source information extraction, followed by workspace construction, collaborative event generation, and multimodal record generation. The following shared instructions are prepended to the system message of each construction call. Shared system instructions You are one worker inside multi-step data-generation pipeline that turns source document into fictional company's internal records (Slack, email, Notion, images, documents) and question set over them. The company is {{V_org_frame}}. Global rules that apply to every step: Temporal span 0 < 1 hour 1 < 24 hours 24 < 48 hours 48 < 72 hours 72 hours Total # 122 261 116 55 223 Share 15.7% 33.6% 14.9% 7.1% 28.7% 777 100.0% Visual content extraction (continued) - text_labels: the short text strings printed inside the image (legend entries, panel titles, callouts). - key_numbers: numbers printed inside the image, excluding axis tick labels. Extraction limits and additional requirements: {{visual_extraction_requirements}} Table 5: Temporal span of gold evidence. For each representative sufficient evidence set, is the difference between the latest and earliest record timestamps. Counts and percentages cover the 777 answerable questions with at least two retrieval records. The median span is 24.0 hours. Shared system instructions (continued) - The source document is RAW MATERIAL, never subject. Nobody in the fictional company knows that paper, article, report or publication exists as such. Never write the excluded terms or any venue name in generated company content, and never use publication-style figure or table numbering. - Numbers and the names of datasets, sources, indicators, metrics, models and methods are taken from the source exactly as given. Never round, never invent number unless the instruction explicitly asks for an invented world-only value, and then mark it as invented. - Output exactly one JSON object and nothing else. No markdown fences, no commentary. - Be concrete and short. Real people write short messages. B.1.1 Source Information Extraction We extract textual and visual information from each seed document, including key values, configurations, claims, and visual facts. The following prompts structure this information for constructing workplace records. Visual content extraction You describe figure precisely and list facts that can only be learned by looking at it. These facts later become questions that cannot be answered from any text, so precision matters more than coverage. ---USER--- Caption of the figure: "{{caption}}" From the attached image, produce: - description: description of what is shown. - image_only_facts: facts reader learns only from the pixels, each with the exact short value string as printed. Do not include facts that the caption already states. Prefer substantive facts (a rank, timestamp, value printed on bar, which curve is highest, what thumbnail shows) over layout trivia (panel letters, axis names, colours). Textual content extraction You read technical document and extract the facts product/research team inside company would work with: what the system is, how it is configured, what it claims with numbers, and the steps of the method. Copy every number exactly as written. ---USER--- Document text: {{doc_text}} Tables already transcribed (for reference; do not repeat their cells as claims unless the text states them): {{tables}} Extract: - method_name: the proposed system's name. - one_sentence: what it does, in product language (no "we propose", no "paper"). - task_summary: the task, the datasets/benchmarks and the metrics. - components: named models, datasets, baselines, modules. - config_facts: configuration / hyper-parameter / setup facts with exact values. - claims: quantitative claims with the exact number strings they rest on, source hint, and label: short noun phrase naming what the leading number measures, written WITHOUT any digit, unit or value. - pipeline_steps: ordered steps of the method as an engineer would list them. Extraction limits and additional requirements: {{extraction_requirements}} B.1.2 Workspace Construction For each project, we define the team, communication channels, access relationships, and milestones. We first select an organization type based on the seed documents content, then generate the corresponding organizational context. This context specifies who participates in the project, where information is shared, and which records each collaborator can access. Organizational archetype selection You look at summary of source document and decide what kind of fictional company would plausibly have produced its content this week. The company will be the document's "author": its Organizational archetype selection (continued) people generate, verify and write up the document's numbers and figures, and nobody in the company knows that publication exists. ---USER--- Title: {{title}} What it is: {{one_sentence}} Task / scope summary: {{task_summary}} Tables: {{tables}} Named components / entities: {{components}} Choose exactly one archetype: - "research_lab": the document reports experiments run by the authors (a proposed method or system evaluated on benchmarks; ablations; baselines). The company is an engineering team shipping that system. - "analysis_firm": the document is report, framework, strategy, survey, forecast, audit or standard whose numbers come from data gathering, modelling or expert judgement rather than from experiments the authors ran. The company is research/analysis consultancy writing this report for client. Return {"archetype": "...", "reason": "one sentence"}. The selected organization type determines the terminology used in the generation prompts. The following table lists examples for research labs and analysis firms. Archetype-dependent terminology Placeholder Research lab Analysis firm V_item V_value V_tracker V_deliverable finding figure run metric Experiment Tracker Evidence Table internal technical report client report Team and communication channel configuration You design small fictional company: {{V_org_frame}}. The content comes from source document, but in this company it is simply the work of the week. You must not mention that publication exists. ---USER--- The work: {{method_name}} -- {{one_sentence}} Scope and measures: {{task_summary}} Named entities in the source (components, datasets, sources, sectors, indicators, baselines): {{components}} Steps of the work: {{pipeline_steps}} Simulation window: {{simulation_window}} Milestone requirements: {{milestone_requirements}} Team requirements: {{team_requirements}} Channel and access requirements: {{channel_requirements}} Team and communication channel configuration (continued) Customer requirements: {{customer_requirements}} New collaborator requirements: {{joiner_requirements}} Names already used: {{avoid_names}} Return: - company_name (invented, not real company), tagline (what they do, size, city), product (what they sell and to whom). - project_codename (an internal codename for this week's deliverable), project_sentence (what the team is finishing this week; refer to the work as the internal {{V_system_word}}), internal_model_name (what people call the {{V_system_word}} in chat; may reuse the source's name). - customer_name, customer_contact (full invented name), customer_contact_email (at an invented domain). - milestone_a (internal), milestone_b (external). - people: people with realistic diverse names and roles. Each has an `owns` sentence tied to parts of the work, `voice`, and colour. - channels: channels with purposes, members, and access restrictions. - late_joiner: the junior who joins at the specified time, with the specified access scope. B.1.3 Collaborative Event Generation within Project Using the extracted source information and organizational context, we plan events that introduce results, identify and correct errors, record decisions, and update work status. An event specifies workplace action performed by collaborator at particular time. The following prompts define these events and their temporal ordering, which guide the generation of project records. Event scheduling You schedule week of work for company team: {{V_org_frame}}. The tables of the source become {{V_items}} that are {{V_item_done}} at concrete times during the week, so that the team's knowledge evolves: early rows of progression table come first, the adopted row comes last. ---USER--- Company: {{company}} -- {{product}}. Internal name of the work: {{internal_model_name}} (the source calls it {{method_name}}). {{V_customer}}: {{customer}}. Milestones: {{milestone_requirements}} People: {{people}} Channels: {{channels}} Days: {{days}} Event scheduling (continued) Errors, corrections, and decisions (continued) Tables: {{tables}} Configuration / setup facts: {{config_facts}} Required release rows: {{release_rows}} Produce: 1. {{V_items}} in chronological order, with kinds "baseline", "progression", "release", and "analysis" as specified. Give each {{V_item}} an owner, completion time, human label (a name for what is measured -- never containing the row's figures or any value) and its dataset. 2. invented -- world-only facts the company would measure for its own product but the source does not contain. Each has concrete value with unit, an owner, the channel it is first posted in, day and time, and rationale tied to the product. Errors, corrections, and decisions You script the human mistakes and the decisions of the week. sections.title: C Quality Control and Human Validation
sections.content: C.1 Workspace Validation Programmatic checks. We first check that each generated output follows the required JSON format and contains the required fields. For extracted numerical claims, we compare the reported values with the source text. We also check that referenced facts, collaborators, and channels exist, that events follow the planned order, and that referenced documents are available. For events involving errors and corrections, we check that each error concerns the intended fact and uses the specified incorrect value. We then verify that the error is introduced, detected, and corrected in the planned order. For Slack messages, we check that each planned event has exactly one corresponding message, sent by the specified collaborator at the specified time. Regeneration with validation feedback. When an output fails validation, we provide the model with the original generation inputs and accumulated validation errors. The model returns revised output and this process continues until the output passes validation or the retry limit is reached. Validation failure feedback ---USER--- Your answer was rejected ({{rejection_count_phrase}} so far). Every one of these must hold at once -- the latest rejection is marked *: {{validation_error_list}} Fix every listed problem without reintroducing an earlier one, and return the full corrected JSON object. Conversational naturalness. For each channel and day with at least six planned events, an LLM reviews the naturalness of the generated Slack conversation. score of 2 or lower on five-point scale, together with reported problems, triggers one additional rewrite. The rewrite uses the original Slack generation prompt with the review feedback, and the resulting messages undergo the same programmatic checks. Slack naturalness review You review day of chat messages for naturalness: do they read like real coworkers, or like script reading numbers aloud? ---USER--- Channel {{channel}}: {{messages}} Score 1-5 (5 = indistinguishable from real team chat). List concrete problems (stilted phrasing, everybody narrating, no reactions, repeated boilerplate, values recited without context). Return {"score": n, "problems": [...]}. The review feedback is appended to the channel context in the Slack generation prompt as follows. Feedback for Slack rewriting reviewer flagged the previous draft: {{reviewer_problems}}. Fix these. C.2 QA Validation Prompts We validate each QA item through three complementary stages: evidence-grounded answering, candidategold comparison, and full-project validation. The first stage produces an independent answer from the cited records, the second compares it with the reference answer, and the third examines the item against all project records. Together, these stages assess evidence sufficiency, answer correctness, question ambiguity, and answerability. C.2.1 Evidence-grounded Answering An independent solver answers the question using only the cited records, without seeing the reference answer. It returns an answer and indicates whether the supplied evidence settles the question. This response provides an initial check of whether the cited records support the requested answer. Evidence-grounded answering The records are the internal records (chat, email, Notion tracker/decisions/meetings, attached documents and images) of one fictional company's project. The benchmark asks questions as the whole team would answer them after the project ended, with every record visible. Output exactly one JSON object and nothing else. You are careful employee answering question from the records given to you. Use only these records; do not guess from general knowledge. Give exact values, names and times as they appear. If the records do not settle the question, say so and set knowable=false (name the closest recorded fact, but do not present it as the answer). Question: {q} Cited records: {cited records} C.2.2 CandidateGold Comparison The comparison stage evaluates the independent answer against the reference answer on the specific object requested by the question. It allows equivalent wording and appropriate rounding while distinguishing substantive disagreements, missing required qualifiers, and incorrect abstention. The resulting judgment is passed to the full-project validation stage alongside the solvers answer. Candidategold comparison Full-project validation (continued) You grade one candidate answer against the gold answer. Procedure: (1) State the asked object: the single thing the question asks for (a value, an entity, time, choice, an explanation's key claim). (2) Compare candidate and gold ONLY on the asked object. Tolerate wording, rounding at the precision the question implies, extra correct detail, and missing secondary explanation. (3) If the gold says the records do not establish the answer: candidate that abstains or says it is not recorded is match; candidate that commits to value is mismatch (cause answered_unanswerable). If the gold gives an answer and the candidate abstains: mismatch (cause candidate_abstained). Return {"asked_object": str, "verdict": "match" "partial" "mismatch", "cause": "none" "different_value" "wrong_entity" "missing_required_part" "candidate_abstained" "answered_unanswerable" "other", "reason": str}. partial = asked object right but required qualifier (unit, one of two required items, direction) wrong or missing. Question: {q} Gold answer: {gold} Gold status: {answerableunanswerable} Candidate answer: {Stage-1 answer} Candidate says knowable: {Stage-1 knowable} C.2.3 Full-project Validation The final stage examines the question, reference answer, and cited evidence against all records of the project. It checks whether the wording admits an equally valid competing answer, whether the reference answers values are supported, whether the answerability label is consistent with the records, and whether the cited evidence is sufficient. The independent solvers response informs this assessment, but does not determine it. The validator returns pass, fix, or drop decision and specifies concrete edits when the item can be repaired. Full-project validation You audit one benchmark item against ALL records of its project. You also see what an independent solver answered when given only the cited records. Decide, reading the records and images yourself: 1. competing_answer: Could careful employee defend materially different answer to the question AS WORDED (a different referent, version, time, or reading of an ambiguous term)? equally_valid is true only if the wording does not let reasonable employee decide which is meant. 2. numbers: For every number, date and time in the gold, check that the records give that value for the thing the gold attaches it to; list any that are wrong or unverifiable. 3. status: If the gold says the records do not establish the answer, check whether some record actually gives what is asked. If the gold gives an answer, check whether the question presupposes something the records contradict. 4. evidence_sufficient: Can the asked object be derived from the cited records alone? The solver's result is hint, not proof. Then give verdict: pass (item is fine) fix (salvageable by concrete edit: wording, gold detail, evidence list) drop (gold wrong or the question cannot be made to pick one answer). category: gold_wrong ambiguous_question evidence_insufficient unanswerable_is_answerable leak none. Return {"competing_answer": {"answer": strnull, "records": [ids], "equally_valid": bool}, "numbers": {"wrong_or_unverified": [str], "note": str}, "status": {"ok": bool, "note": str}, "evidence_sufficient": bool, "verdict": str, "category": str, "fix": {"q": strnull, "gold": strnull, "evidence_add": [ids]} null, "note": str} Question: {q} Gold answer: {gold} Gold status: {answerableunanswerable} Solution: {solution-stage JSON} Cited records: {evidence ids + solution record_ids, deduplicated} Stage-1 solver: answer='{Stage-1 answer}' knowable={...} -> grade {matchpartialmismatch} ({cause}): {reason} Cited records: {cited records} All project records: {full project records} C.3 Human Validation Interface We conducted human evaluation using an annotation interface that displayed one benchmark item at time. The interface comprised four main components: Question. The question was displayed at the top of the interface to establish the information being requested. Reference answer. The reference answer appeared directly below the question. Annotators assessed whether it correctly answered the question. Cited evidence. Supporting records were presented as individually expandable cards. Annotators inspected these records one by one to determine whether, taken together, they supFigure 2: Human Evaluation Interface. Annotators inspect the question, reference answer, and expandable evidence records with source metadata, then assess evidence derivability (C1), answer correctness (C2), and the absence of answer leakage in the question (C3). An optional comment field allows annotators to explain their judgments or flag ambiguities. ported the reference answer. Source metadata, such as application names, filenames, page numbers, message authors, and timestamps, enabled annotators to identify the provenance of each record. searchable source browser provided additional context and highlighted the cited evidence. Assessment panel. Annotators recorded their judgments using three criteria: C1: Derivable from evidence. Can the reference answer be derived using only the highlighted evidence records? C2: Answer correct. Is the reference answer correct for what the question asks? C3: No leak. Is the requested answer absent from the question text? Premise values, incorrect values explicitly being questioned, and run identifiers were not considered answer leakage. For C1 and C2, annotators selected Yes, No, or Cannot judge. For C3, they indicated whether the answer was absent from or present in the question. An optional comment field allowed annotators to explain their judgments or flag ambiguities. After completing the assessment, annotators saved their responses and proceeded to the next item.
